standard.title: Indirect evaluation devices
standard.description: understand how evaluation can be expressed directly and indirectly using devices such as allusion, evocative vocabulary and metaphor
standard.prior_knowledge: Students recognise evaluative language and understand how evaluations are substantiated by textual evidence (AC9E7LA02). They have not yet examined how evaluation can be embedded indirectly through literary devices that position readers without explicit appraisal language.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how evaluation is expressed both directly and indirectly through devices including allusion, evocative vocabulary and metaphor.

nodes.label: Direct vs indirect evaluation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between evaluations expressed directly (explicit appraisal language) and those embedded indirectly through word choice and framing.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example of direct evaluation and one of indirect evaluation in a text, and explain how they differ in the way they communicate the author's position.
nodes.typical_width: Compare direct and indirect evaluation across two text types (e.g. editorial and advertisement, podcast and poem), explaining how each mode positions the reader differently.
wider: Analyse how advertising deliberately avoids direct evaluative claims while using indirect devices to position consumers
Compare the evaluative intensity of direct versus indirect appraisal in political speech, examining which is more persuasive and why

response_modes.reason: Students default to identifying explicit evaluative language ('great', 'terrible') and miss indirect embedding. Comparing diverse text types — especially non-literary ones like advertisements — reveals the fuller range of how evaluation works.

nodes.hinge_reason: The direct/indirect distinction is a prerequisite for N2 and N3 — students who cannot identify indirect evaluation cannot analyse evocative vocabulary or metaphor as evaluative devices at those nodes.
success_criteria: Student identifies at least one direct and one indirect evaluation in a text
Student explains how indirect evaluation positions the reader without using explicit appraisal terms

nodes.label: Evocative vocabulary as evaluative device
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how evocative vocabulary choices embed evaluation — directing readers' views without stating an explicit appraisal.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify evocative word choices in a text and explain how they guide the reader's evaluation of a person, place or idea.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how a range of evocative vocabulary choices in a text work together to build an implicit evaluative position, drawing on examples from print, editorial, talkback or podcast contexts.
wider: Compare evocative vocabulary in texts covering the same event from different publication contexts (broadsheet vs tabloid, mainstream vs community media)
Examine how similes used in evaluative contexts carry embedded judgement through the connotations of the vehicle term

response_modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of evocative vocabulary examples across contexts to understand this as a systematic device rather than an occasional stylistic choice. Range across text types matters here.

success_criteria: Student identifies evocative vocabulary and explains the connotations that make the evaluation implicit
Student explains how the word choice directs the reader's view without making the evaluation explicit

nodes.label: Metaphor and allusion as evaluative devices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how metaphor and allusion express evaluation by importing connotations from outside the immediate text to position readers toward particular interpretations.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a metaphor or allusion in a text and explain how it embeds evaluation through the associations it activates.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how metaphor and allusion work as evaluative devices in at least two text types, explaining how the imported associations direct the reader's appraisal.
wider: Analyse how sustained metaphors in editorials or long-form journalism construct an evaluative framework throughout a text
Examine how allusions to shared cultural or literary references position readers who recognise them versus those who don't, as a mechanism of cultural evaluation
Compare how First Nations Australian authors may use allusion to Country and cultural knowledge as evaluative framing in ways that position readers differently

response_modes.reason: The evaluative function of metaphor is not self-evident — students need a reasoning scaffold to move from 'this is a metaphor' to 'this metaphor imports these connotations which direct the reader toward this evaluation'. The chain from vehicle to association to evaluative effect needs explicit modelling.

This node integrates all three indirect devices — allusion, evocative vocabulary, metaphor — as related members of the same evaluative toolkit. Students are assembling a coherent understanding of indirect evaluation as a system.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Metaphor and allusion are richly layered and connect across Literary and Literacy strands. Advancing students can explore how culturally situated allusions create in-group/out-group positioning — an extension into critical literacy that stays within Y9 scope.
success_criteria: Student identifies a metaphor or allusion and names the associations it activates
Student explains how those associations constitute an implicit evaluation of a person, event or idea
